body.text: According to official statements, India is in the midst of an infrastructure boom. In a press release dated June 9, 2026, the Central government declared: “After 2014, infrastructure development has increasingly focused on scale, integration, and long-term capacity creation…. Public capital expenditure increased from about Rs.2 lakh crore in FY2014-15 to Rs.12.2 lakh crore in FY2026-27.”

It added: “This reflects sustained focus on long-term infrastructure creation across sectors. Major programmes such as Sagarmala, Bharatmala, PM GatiShakti, PMAY, Jal Jeevan Mission, PM Ujjwala Yojana, and UDAN expanded infrastructure access. These initiatives linked infrastructure growth with household welfare, economic opportunity, and regional development.”

There have clearly been some high-profile projects undertaken and completed, such as major expressways linking cities. Most of the public infrastructure projects have related to surface transport, specifically, roads, rail, bridges, tunnels, and urban metro systems. There are also projects related to “smart cities” and digital connectivity, although these appear to have been much less significant in terms of actual public spending. The other significant approach to infrastructure has been increased reliance on the private corporate sector, through both privatisation of existing public assets such as airports and some railway stations, and public-private partnerships.

At the macroeconomic level, public infrastructure spending, especially in a lower-middle-income country like India, is widely seen to be positive for current economic activity, future growth, and socio-economic development.

A positive link between public and private investment has been found in several cross-country studies. This is because public investment typically eases supply constraints through reducing infrastructural bottlenecks, creating direct and indirect demand for private investment in ancillary activities, and through more economic activity in the affected areas and sectors.

Public investment is seen to be crucial for infrastructure development because markets on their own do not generate the returns required by private investors. It typically involves lumpy front-loaded spending with returns that come in later and often with externalities and positive spillovers that cannot be captured by individual private investors.

Therefore, if the country is indeed in the midst of an infrastructure boom, it could be expected that there would be a significant increase in private investment, and in the aggregate investment rate in the economy too.

In India, where decades of underinvestment in infrastructure despite high rates of aggregate economic growth have left the country relatively poorly provided compared with other BRICS countries, it is even more likely that such a boost in public infrastructure spending would result in a higher investment rate.

This is all the more so since the government claims that this boom has apparently operated since 2014 so that the time lags (of three to five years) usually estimated for infrastructure projects would also have been taken care of.
Actual pattern of investment

This is why it is quite surprising to see the actual pattern of investment (or gross fixed capital formation) in the country over the period since 2012. Chart 1 traces the investment rate as a share of GDP since 2012–13, and the relative shares of public and private investment.

It is startling to see that the investment rate (or gross fixed capital formation as a share of GDP) declined continuously from its peak of nearly 35 per cent of GDP in 2011–12 to only 28 per cent in 2017–18, fluctuated at a lower level thereafter, and even after rising again from 2021, remained significantly below the peak level around 30 per cent in 2023–24.

Furthermore, even this declining investment rate was essentially sustained by public investment, particularly from 2015–16 to 2018–19, and then again more recently. In fact, another study, by Knight Frank, using Central and State government budget data and private corporate balance sheet data, found that the private share of total capital expenditure collapsed from more than half in 2011 to less than 5 per cent in 2023 (Chart 2). This goes against both received wisdom and the presumed expectations of the government and definitely requires more explanation.
Why did increased public investment in infrastructure, and the many projects touted by the Narendra Modi government, not have more substantial outcomes in terms of private investment?

There are many elements of the possible answer to this conundrum. First, private investment includes both private corporate investment and household investment. While the exact break-up for these years is not available, in the past household investment (which includes not only construction by household enterprises but also investment by small and micro enterprises) constituted a significant part of total private investment.

It is well known that small and micro enterprises have suffered a series of major blows over this period, from demonetisation to GST to extreme and harshly implemented COVID-19 lockdowns without compensation, so it would be no surprise if their investment declined and/or did not recover easily.

However, that does not explain the lack of response of private companies. So, the second point to note is that all business investment, especially private corporate investment, responds to demand conditions and the expected size of the market. Domestic mass consumption demand has been dampened by all of the factors mentioned above. The significant investments that have occurred have been concentrated among the largest conglomerates, often linked to privatisation or special privileges accruing to favoured business houses. Indeed, total corporate profits have also been disproportionately skewed towards such companies. But even if some of them have increased their investment, this has obviously not been enough to counteract the declining tendencies among other segments of capital.

Third, while there has certainly been more public investment, especially in high visibility big-ticket projects since 2014, it is not the case that nothing was done earlier. Indeed, the decline in the aggregate investment rate after 2012 suggests that there was more public and private investment relative to GDP before the Modi regime came to power.

So, despite the hype surrounding every newly declared infrastructure project, while there has been some increase in public infrastructure investment compared with the pre-2014 pattern, in the aggregate it has probably not been that great. Rather, past projects were more widely spread across different sizes and locations and undertaken with less publicity compared with the current regime.

Fourth, there have been significant delays in many projects. One estimate by Knight Frank is that infrastructure projects accounted for 95 per cent of the 779 delayed public projects in 2024. Of these, the bulk of the delays were in road transport. Delays also tend to be associated with cost overruns, although in this regard Railways projects showed the largest cost overruns of nearly 50 per cent in 2024.

Fifth, and this may be a more important factor than is generally recognised, the poor quality of much of the recently built road infrastructure has meant that not all of it would necessarily be a future asset or a positive contribution to the economy.

There is a serious lack of regulatory scrutiny and monitoring of implementation, especially when contractors close to the governments or local bodies concerned are involved. There have been many cases of substandard materials being used and contractors who have clearly failed to deliver the required quality in some projects being chosen again for other projects.
The emphasis on speedy completion of projects, often because a date has been set for inauguration by the Prime Minister or some other high official, has been blamed for some defects as well.

As a result of all this, the recent record of breakdowns, collapses, and other malfunctions and failures of important infrastructure projects is shocking. A media report said that there have been 170 bridge collapses in the four years between 2021 and 2025, with Bihar, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Gujarat topping the list.

These killed more than 200 people, but they also meant that the bridges became unusable for significant periods, and some are still out of commission. Collapses of newly constructed or under-construction bridges and roads, as well as airport canopies, have also become common.

Recently in Uttar Pradesh, an under-construction flyover collapsed in Varanasi, killing at least 16 people. Sections of newly inaugurated roads like the Lucknow-Kanpur elevated expressway and the Ganga Expressway have shown major cracks and have even caved in.

There have also been some surprising cases of major design flaws, such as the Aishbagh Overbridge in Bhopal, built at a cost of Rs.18 crore, which features a sharp 90-degree turn that renders it quite unsafe for traffic, or the Gokhale Bridge in Mumbai that was rebuilt after an earlier collapse with a 6 foot gap between the new segment and an existing flyover.
Lack of accountability

The lack of accountability in all such cases and the repeat awarding of contracts to those who have already been associated with failed projects or collapses mean that such problems are not only about design and engineering issues; they also reflect corruption, inadequate auditing, and a rush to complete projects that will enable leaders to hold grand inaugurations (often just before elections). All this, in turn, means that the data provided in official handouts of massive infrastructure expansion is open to question, if only because of quality concerns.

In addition to direct public investment, there has been an increasing emphasis on privatisation and public-private partnerships for infrastructure development. The latter should be recognised for what they are: direct or indirect subsidies to (typically large) private corporate players. They usually involve public subsidies for private investors, in the form of preferential bank credit access and “viability gap funding” (VGF), to ensure private corporate investment and continued participation.

In 2024–25, there were 72 such VGF schemes, estimated to cost the public exchequer around Rs.46,256 crore. Meanwhile, privatisation—including the controversial privatisation of several publicly owned airports to conglomerates whose owners are seen to be close to the ruling regime—is supposed to lead to improvements in infrastructure, but the evidence on this is mixed at best.

Other recently developed financing instruments include REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts that own and manage revenue-generating commercial real estate) and InvITs (Infrastructure Investment Trusts that own and operate large public infrastructure projects).

REITs focus on physical buildings, with earnings dependent on lease renewals and tenant occupancy. InvITs focus on heavy public utility structures that typically rely on long-term government contracts, traffic volume, or power grid usage. These raise funds from the public and are subject to regulation by the Securities and Exchange Board of India. Once again, these have raised less money than was hoped for.

Essentially, the problems with India’s recent infrastructure push are similar to the problems with broader economic and social policy over the past decade and more: an obsession with form and display over substance; a focus on short-term gains rather than building for the long term; a predilection for grandiose and highly visible interventions rather than the systematic, solid, and careful policies that would ensure sustainable and inclusive infrastructure for the country and its people.

Jayati Ghosh taught economics at Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, for nearly 35 years, and since January 2021, she has been a professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, US. She has authored and/or edited 21 books and 240 scholarly articles.
